paper_metadata.title: Pricing Multiasset Derivatives by Variational Quantum Algorithms

summary: The paper proposes a variational quantum algorithm for multi‑asset derivative pricing by solving the discretized Black–Scholes PDE with variational quantum simulation and estimating prices via a SWAP‑test inner product. Numerical demonstrations are performed on noiseless simulations for a single‑asset double barrier option using 4–6 qubits, with Euler time step 2.5×10⁻⁵ and parameters r=0.001, σ=0.3, T=1, showing agreement with classical finite‑difference and analytical solutions. The authors claim an asymptotic complexity improvement from O((1/ε)^{O(d)}) for classical FDM to O(1/ε² · (log(1/ε))^d) measurement scaling under certain assumptions.

experiments.description: Variational quantum simulation of the Black–Scholes PDE for pricing a single-asset double knock-out barrier option, with the derivative price recovered via a SWAP-test inner product between the evolved payoff state and the asset-price probability state.

algorithm.variant: variational quantum simulation (VQS) for linear ODEs applied to discretized BSPDE
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient layered ansatz with repeated RY gates and CZ entanglement layers
algorithm.optimizer: L-BFGS-B (for initial-state fidelity maximization in a separate feasibility test); Euler method used for time stepping of variational parameters

hyperparameters.ansatz_parameters: n(m+1) parameters for n qubits and m layers

algorithm.parameter_initialization: VQS starts from parameters corresponding to the identity at tau=0; initial-state feasibility test uses optimization over theta0

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Grid values of the discretized asset-price PDE are encoded in amplitudes over an n-qubit register with Ngr = 2^n grid points; probability distribution state and payoff state are prepared as amplitude-encoded vectors
problem_formulation.objective_function: Price the derivative by solving the Black–Scholes PDE backward in time and computing V0 ≃ e^{-r t_ter} <p(t_ter)|V(t_ter)>
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Barrier conditions handled through boundary terms in the discretized PDE; SWAP test used to estimate overlap instead of extracting a single amplitude

problem_instance.description: Single-asset double knock-out barrier option under the Black–Scholes model

dataset_specification.benchmark_name: analytical double-barrier option formula used as reference
dataset_specification.preprocessing: finite-difference discretization of the Black–Scholes PDE; no log transform

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize asset price interval [l,u] into ngr grids; compare VQS output against classical FDM and analytical solution
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical simulation on a simulator; compare estimated prices against analytical solution and classical FDM; initial-state approximation validated by fidelity maximization

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical finite-difference method; analytical barrier-option formula; L-BFGS-B for initial-state fitting
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical probability density for geometric Brownian motion; discretization of BSPDE; Euler integration for variational parameter dynamics
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: SWAP-test overlap converted to price by square root and discounting

speedup_claims.factor: polynomial in d and 1/ϵ for the quantum part; avoids (1/ϵ)^{O(d)} bottleneck in price extraction
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical finite-difference method and prior amplitude-extraction-based quantum PDE solvers
speedup_claims.conditions: assuming efficient state preparation and the stated VQS/SWAP-test framework; under the paper's assumptions for boundary-state generation and bounded norms
speedup_claims.caveats: Overall complexity is heuristic because VQS is heuristic; SWAP-test measurements still scale as O(1/ϵ^2 (log(1/ϵ))^d) under stated assumptions; no end-to-end runtime advantage is experimentally benchmarked on hardware.

speedup_claims.conditions: when function values on (1/ϵ)^{O(d)} grid points are encoded into O(d log(1/ϵ)) qubits
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a resource-scaling claim, not a hardware benchmark.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(d log(1/ϵ))) gates for VQS; SWAP-test measurements O(1/ϵ^2 (log(1/ϵ))^d) under stated assumptions
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical FDM: O((1/ϵ)^{O(d)}) time and space

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: not provided; complexity improvement only asymptotic vs classical FDM
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require circuits with O(d log(1/ε)) qubits and poly(d log(1/ε)) gates plus many SWAP-test measurements; practical advantage would require large logical quantum computers and efficient state preparation.
limiting_factors: Results only demonstrated on noiseless classical simulation
Problem size limited to 1 asset with 4–6 qubits
State preparation of payoff and probability distributions assumed but not implemented
Variational convergence and measurement overhead not characterized at scale
Complexity advantage relies on asymptotic analysis and assumptions

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states numerical calculations/simulations and does not name a real QPU.

num_qubits not explicitly given for the main experiment; inferred only that the register size is n qubits with Ngr = 2^n grid points, but exact n for the main numerical run is not stated in the text excerpt.
Circuit depth is not explicitly quantified; the paper reports an ansatz with m layers and n(m+1) parameters, but no total depth number is given.
The authors claim potential speedup vs classical FDM in asymptotic complexity (removing (1/ε)^{O(d)} dependence), but only numerical simulations on small systems are performed.

experiments.description: Feasibility test for preparing the initial payoff state of a single-asset call option by optimizing a one-parameter ansatz to match the discretized payoff vector.

algorithm.variant: initial-state fidelity maximization with a one-parameter hardware-efficient ansatz
algorithm.ansatz: ansatz shown in Fig. 1 with six qubits and six layers

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Discretized payoff values encoded as amplitudes over a 6-qubit register
problem_formulation.objective_function: Approximate |Vbar(0)> = sum_k f_pay(x(k))|k> by an ansatz state

problem_instance.description: Single-asset call option payoff-state preparation test

dataset_specification.preprocessing: discretized asset-price grid with l=0.5, u=2

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Construct target amplitude vector from payoff function on discretized grid
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Fidelity maximization; reported fidelity error |1 - alpha0^-2 |<Vbar(0)|nu(theta0)>|^2| <= 1.2e-5

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct target payoff vector from analytical payoff function
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute fidelity and compare to target state

speedup_claims.caveats: This is only a feasibility test for state preparation; no speedup analysis is provided.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Demonstration only shows feasibility of preparing payoff state with a 6‑qubit ansatz; no comparison to classical algorithms.
limiting_factors: No comparison to classical state-preparation methods
Optimization performed offline with classical optimizer

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper reports a numerical optimization/simulation study and no physical device.
Speedup order is not analyzed for this feasibility sub-experiment; only state-preparation fidelity is reported.
